Curry's Paradox

ParadoxesAreaSequences
Game: Two pieces are swapped inside a triangle and some area seems to appear out of nowhere; there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag the coloured pieces from the top triangle into the same places in the bottom one, or press Animate. Then compare the leftover rectangles.

Pieces
Hole is
Look for the math

Cut a thin right triangle with legs 13 and 5 into two small triangles and a rectangle. Swap the triangles and the leftover rectangle grows from 15 to 16 squares. Where did the extra square come from?

Fibonacci numbers

The numbers are consecutive Fibonacci numbers. A triangle with legs Fn+1 and Fn−1 holds triangles with legs Fn, Fn−2 and Fn−1, Fn−3, and rectangles Fn−1 × Fn−2 and Fn × Fn−3. Their areas always differ by one: FnFn−3 − Fn−1Fn−2 = (−1)n, a form of Cassini’s identity and a case of d’Ocagne’s identity Fn+1Fm − FnFm+1 = (−1)nFm−n with m = n − 2. The logic test checked both identities, with indices from −12 to 12, and the areas for every size the applet offers.

The resolution

The three slanted edges are not on one line: the big triangle's edge has slope 5/13 ≈ 0.385, but the small triangle's is 2/5 = 0.4 and the larger one's 3/8 = 0.375. So the "triangle" is really a thin four-sided shape that bulges a little one way in the first arrangement and dents the other way in the second, and in each the sliver between the pieces and the line is worth half a square: the pieces fall half a square short of the triangle in one and exceed it by half a square in the other, a total difference of exactly one. For larger n the slopes agree better and better, so you cannot see it; the dashed red line shows the true hypotenuse, and with n = 4 the gap is obvious. The test confirmed the half-square slack for every size.

Four pieces and the hole

With n = 6 the 5 × 3 rectangle can be cut into two shapes that tile the 8 × 2 rectangle with a single unit square missing, inside it or on its edge (Curry’s own version): 15 squares of material cannot fill 16. This is closely related to the missing square puzzle.

Set n = 4 (the smallest) and swap the triangles: see how far the pieces bend away from the red line. Then try n = 11 and look for any gap at all.
